bib.title: Hallucination of Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed only for lineage (from ref [38] onward not read line by line).

question: What causes hallucination in multimodal LLMs, how is it evaluated, and how can it be mitigated?
contributions: A layered, granular taxonomy of MLLM hallucination causes (data, model, training, inference)
Overview of metrics and benchmarks, with a comparison of mainstream MLLMs on generative and discriminative benchmarks
Mitigation methods organised by the cause they address

results.claim: Hallucination in MLLMs is mainly cross-modal inconsistency between generated text and the image, and studies focus on object hallucination in three types: category, attribute, relation.
results.quote: Hallucination of MLLM generally refers to the phenomenon where the generated text response does not align with the corresponding visual content.

results.claim: Causes of MLLM hallucination are grouped as data (quantity, quality, statistical bias), model (weak vision model, language prior, weak interface), training (next-token loss, no RLHF stage) and inference (diluted visual attention, trap visual tokens).
results.quote: Hallucinations have multifaceted origins, spanning the entire spectrum of MLLMs’ capability acquisition process.

results.claim: CHAIR_i is the fraction of mentioned objects that are hallucinated; CHAIR_s is the fraction of sentences with a hallucinated object; restricted to the 80 MSCOCO objects.
results.quote: In the paper of CHAIR [137], the range of objects is restricted to the 80 MSCOCO objects.

results.claim: POPE turns hallucination evaluation into yes/no object-existence probing on 500 MSCOCO images with random, popular and adversarial negative sampling.
results.note: Table 1 lists POPE size as 3,000 (questions per subset presumably); text says 500 images.
results.quote: drawing 500 images from the MSCOCO dataset

results.claim: AMBER Score combines CHAIR (generative) and F1 (discriminative) into one score.
MMHal-Bench has 96 image-question pairs over 8 question categories x 12 object topics, rated by GPT-4.
results.quote: Comprising 96 image-question pairs, ranging in 8 question categories × 12 object topics

results.claim: HallusionBench has 455 visual-question control pairs, 346 figures and 1129 questions, split into Visual Dependent and Visual Supplement.
results.quote: It consists of 455 visual-question control pairs, with 346 different figures and a total of 1129 questions

results.claim: GPT-4V has the lowest CHAIR (4.3, lower is better) and highest AMBER Score (92.7) among models in the generative comparison; open models like CogVLM reach 7.9 / 86.1 and LLaVA-1.5 7B 8.6 / 82.9.
results.source: numbers copied from original benchmark papers
results.setup: Table 2, generative benchmarks, numbers from original papers, not rerun
results.table: Table 2, row GPT-4V, column AMBER Score (CHAIR 4.3)

results.claim: mPLUG-Owl (7B) has CHAIR 23.1 and AMBER Score 54.1, the weakest of the models with both entries in Table 2.
results.table: Table 2, row mPLUG-Owl, column CHAIR (On AMBER)

results.claim: Benchmarks do not rank models consistently: performance differs across benchmarks because dimensions and emphases differ.
results.quote: We observe that the MLLMs’ performance is not always consistent across different benchmarks.

results.claim: In the discriminative comparison, training-free decoding methods on LLaVA-1.5 7B lift POPE F1; DAC(LLaVA-1.5) has the highest POPE random F1 shown (90.60) vs 83.44 for plain LLaVA-1.5 7B.
results.note: Table 3 header prints 'POPE Random' twice; the middle column is presumably Popular.
results.table: Table 3, row DAC(LLaVA-1.5), POPE first column (83.44 for row LLaVA-1.5)

results.claim: Higher vision-encoder resolution generally lowers hallucination on CCEval (CLIP-ViT-L-112, 224, 336 compared in HallE-Switch).
results.quote: higher resolution generally results in lower degrees of hallucination

results.claim: An oracle study in HALC found decoding from the optimal visual contexts eliminates over 84.5% of hallucinations.
results.setup: Oracle study, optimal visual context per token
results.quote: decoding from the provided optimal visual contexts eliminates over 84.5% of hallucinations

results.claim: CIEM's LLM-generated QA data has an error rate of around 5%.
results.setup: LLM-generated QA pairs from image descriptions
results.quote: empirical result shows that the generated data has low error rate, around 5%

results.claim: Models trained on mostly positive instruction data tend to answer Yes to any instruction, causing hallucination.
results.quote: current models tend to answer "Yes" for any instructions presented to the model, even when a proper answer should be "No"

results.claim: Statistical bias: frequent objects (person) and co-occurrence (refrigerator-microwave) drive false Yes answers; more data may alleviate but cannot fully resolve it.
results.quote: Increasing the scale of data may alleviate the effect, but cannot fully resolve it, given the long-tail distribution of the real world.

results.claim: Authors say benchmarks lack standards; POPE yes/no does not match human use and generative benchmarks depend on external models.
results.quote: The lack of standardized benchmarks and evaluation metrics poses significant challenges in assessing the degree of hallucination in MLLMs.

results.claim: LLaVA to LLaVA-1.5 scaled the vision encoder from CLIP-ViT-L-224 to CLIP-ViT-L-336 with considerable gain.
results.quote: scale up the CLIP ViT vision encoder from CLIP-ViT-L-224 to CLIP-ViT-L-336

limits: Survey: no experiments of its own; Tables 2 and 3 copy numbers from the original benchmark papers, so setups (prompts, decoding) are not controlled and many cells are empty.
Scope is object hallucination in visual-to-text generation; unified understanding and generation models, other modalities and factuality hallucination are out of focus.
Authors concede the field is at an early stage, benchmarks lack standards, and detail level of training data is an open question.
The authors say methods rely on empirical observation and mechanisms are poorly understood (Sec 6.6).
Version dated April 2025; later methods are not covered.
practices: Include negative instructions and reject-answer data in instruction tuning so models do not say Yes to everything (Sec 3.1.2, 5.1.1).
Use human-annotated QA data alongside GPT-generated instruction data to reduce noise (Sec 3.1.2).
Scale up vision-encoder resolution, e.g. 224 to 336, to reduce hallucination (Sec 5.2.1).
Complement CLIP with other encoders or tool models (DINO, OCR, detection, segmentation) to recover lost visual detail (Sec 5.2.2).
Use preference optimisation (DPO) with hallucinated vs accurate response pairs, or RLHF with fine-grained human feedback (Sec 5.3.2).
Use contrastive or visual-amplifying decoding (VCD, M3ID, OPERA) as training-free mitigation at inference (Sec 5.4.1).
Avoid generating the paragraph break token, or instruct single-paragraph output, to lower hallucination (Sec 5.4.1, Others).
Use post-hoc correction pipelines (Woodpecker, LURE, Volcano, VFC) that verify claims against the image (Sec 5.4.5).
Report both discriminative (POPE-style yes/no) and generative (CHAIR, LLM-judged) metrics because rankings differ between benchmarks (Sec 4, 6.4).
For caption evaluation, add a coverage metric because CHAIR favours short captions (CCEval, Sec 4).

terms.definition: Generated text describes objects, attributes or relations inconsistent with the image; three types: category, attribute, relation.
the discrepancy between generated content and verifiable real-world facts
the divergence of generated content from user instructions or the context provided by the input, as well as self-consistency within generated content
proportion of words generated that are actually in the image; per-instance CHAIR_i and per-sentence CHAIR_s
Pooling-based Object Probing Evaluation: yes/no questions about probing objects with random, popular, adversarial negative sampling
knowledge in the LLM that can override visual content (e.g. red banana answered as yellow)
contrast output distributions from original and distorted visual inputs to suppress bias and language priors
first allowing the MLLM to generate a text response and then identifying and eliminating hallucinating content
MLLM answers plausibly when the desired answer is I don't know
